h1: Moving from a brewpub to packaged beer and the decisions involved
title: Moving From Brewpub to Packaged Beer | Craft Beer School
desc: What changes when a brewpub in India starts selling packaged beer: licences, equipment, shelf life, pricing and the questions to settle before you buy a line.
teaser: Your beer sells out every weekend. That does not mean it will sell from a warm shelf three states away.
standfirst: Taking beer out of the brewpub and into cans or bottles changes almost everything: the licence, the kit, the quality standard and the economics. Here are the decisions to settle first.
sections:
A brewpub's beer sales are capped by seats and opening hours. Packaged beer promises reach: retail shelves, other bars, homes. It also promises brand visibility far beyond one neighbourhood. Those are good reasons. They are also reasons that hide a different business inside the one you already run.

A brewpub sells fresh beer at full price to guests in its own room. A packaging brewery sells beer that must survive transport, storage and time, through a route to market where others take a margin. Treat the move as starting a second business that shares a brewhouse.

In many Indian states, a microbrewery or brewpub licence allows beer to be sold for consumption on the premises only. Packaging for retail sale usually needs a different licence category, label and brand registration with the excise department, MRP approval and sometimes a different site. Some states have allowed limited takeaway such as growlers, which we explain in takeaway beer rules in India.

Find out exactly what your state permits before spending anything on equipment. Rules vary by state and change, so work with a licensing consultant and read the current notification.

Kegs to other bars are often the gentlest first step: draught beer, chilled, consumed within weeks. Cans and bottles reach further but demand more. Our guide to kegs versus cans as a business choice compares them. In short:

  • Kegs. Lower packaging cost per litre, but you need kegs, a washer and a system to track and recover them.
  • Cans. Light, block light completely, popular with craft drinkers. Printed cans carry large minimum orders.
  • Bottles. Familiar to Indian retail, heavier to ship, breakable and vulnerable to light unless brown.

Brewpub beer is often served within days of leaving the tank, so small oxygen pickups and short shelf life go unnoticed. Packaged beer has to taste right weeks later after sitting in Indian heat. That means low dissolved oxygen at packaging, carbonation to spec, a clear decision on filtration and pasteurisation and a forced ageing test before you set a best-before date. It also means a basic QC lab and someone responsible for release.

A hazy IPA that tastes brilliant at your tap and stale on a warm shelf damages the brand more than not packaging at all.

In the brewpub you capture the full retail price. In packaged beer you share it with distributors, retailers and the state through excise and taxes. You also pay for packaging, logistics and breakage. Our beer packaging costs guide lists the cost lines. Build a per-unit cost and a price waterfall from brewery gate to MRP before committing. If the margin left for you is thin, you need volume. Volume needs capacity, cash and a sales team.
Testing the market before the line

You do not have to buy a canning or bottling line to find out whether packaged beer sells. Contract packing at another brewery, a mobile canning service where one exists or a limited run of kegs to friendly bars can test demand with far less capital. Each of those still needs the right licences and labels, so the paperwork comes first either way.

Use the test to learn what a guide cannot tell you: which beer travels best, how fast it sells away from your own room, how retailers store it and what breaks or goes stale. A few months of real sales data makes the decision about a line far less of a gamble.

Also watch what happens at the pub. If tank time goes to packaged beer and the taps run dry on a Saturday, the test has taught you about capacity too.
Decisions to settle before you buy

1. What does our licence allow? What new licences would we need?
  2. Kegs, cans or bottles first? In what volume per month?
  3. Do we have the brewhouse and tank capacity without starving the pub?
  4. Who will sell the beer? Through which route to market?
  5. What shelf life can we prove? How will we keep it cold?
  6. Can we test with a contract packer or mobile canner before buying a line?

Settling these questions with real numbers is what separates a packaging launch that grows the business from one that drains it.
faqs: Can a brewpub in India sell packaged beer?
Many brewpub licences only allow on-site consumption. Packaging for retail usually needs a different licence and brand registration. Check your state's current rules with a licensing consultant.
Should I start with kegs or cans?
Kegs to other bars are often the gentler first step because the beer stays cold and is drunk quickly. Cans reach further but need tighter quality control and larger minimum orders.
What is the biggest quality risk in packaged beer?
Oxygen picked up at packaging, which shortens shelf life, combined with warm storage on the way to the drinker.
